subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: Water on Earth — Identifying freshwater sources from images and writing their names (p. 5)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a large glass of water on the board and a tiny teaspoon beside it, telling students that if all Earth's water filled the glass, freshwater would barely fill the teaspoon. Students share what they already know about water around them — rivers, ponds, rain, oceans — and the teacher records their ideas in two columns: salty and fresh.

Students open Textbook p. 4 and the teacher poses the two discussion questions: Can we drink ocean water? What can ocean water be used for? Small groups talk briefly, then share back. The teacher guides students to see that salty water cannot be used for drinking or growing crops, making freshwater precious and rare.

Students turn to Textbook p. 5 and examine the images of freshwater sources. Working individually, they identify each source and write its name in their notebooks. The teacher circulates and asks students to say whether each source is easy or difficult to reach in their own area.

The class comes together and the teacher introduces Johads — small community-built dams in Rajasthan that collect rainwater and refill groundwater. The teacher asks: Why would a community spend time building something like this? Students connect the scarcity idea from the teaspoon analogy to the need for such structures, closing on the idea that communities have always found ways to protect freshwater.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between saltwater and freshwater sources and explain why freshwater is a limited and essential resource.
periods.section_context: Teaspoon-in-a-glass analogy for freshwater scarcity, ocean water, textbook images of freshwater sources, Johads of Rajasthan.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'If you could only keep water from one source and all others disappeared, which would you keep and why?' Prompt students from arid or coastal regions to share local water experiences — answers about Johads or traditional wells are especially worth drawing out.

periods.activity_title: Ice, Water, Steam — Watching Water Change
periods.textbook_anchor: Water has Different Forms — Observing condensation, melting, and state changes using a steel glass with ice cubes and a structured observation table (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: The teacher places a dry steel glass on a desk at the front and asks students to predict what will happen on the outside of the glass when ice is placed inside. Students whisper their predictions to a partner before sharing aloud.

Students open Textbook p. 6 and follow the activity instructions. Each group places ice cubes in the steel glass, dries the outside carefully with a cloth, and watches closely. They record observations in response to the three questions on the page: where the water droplets come from, what happens to the ice over time, and what heating water would do. Students note their observations in their notebooks using the structured table — Ice melting / Water boiling / Water left in sunlight for three days.

Groups share their observations in turn. The teacher draws a simple three-box diagram on the board — solid, liquid, vapour — and invites students to place each change they observed into the right box. The class discusses how water can move between all three forms and return to liquid again.

Students write one sentence for each form of water in their notebooks — naming it, describing how it looks or feels, and giving one place in nature where they would find it (e.g., river, snowcapped mountain, clouds). The teacher asks: 'If water can change form and come back, does it ever really disappear?' to leave an open idea about continuity in nature.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how the same material changes between states under different conditions and describe those changes in their own words.
periods.section_context: Steel glass, ice cubes, condensation on glass surface, ice melting, water boiling, water evaporating in sunlight, three states of water.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage close looking before students write — ask 'What do you notice on the outside of the glass before anything else?' Pair students who record confidently with those who need prompting so that notebook entries reflect genuine observation rather than copying.

periods.activity_title: The Bag That Rains — Modelling the Water Cycle
periods.textbook_anchor: Water Cycle — Sealing coloured water in a transparent bag, placing it in sunlight, and recording observations and questions in an I Observe / I Wonder table (p. 7)
materials: Transparent zip-lock or sealed plastic bags (one per group)
Coloured water (water with a few drops of food colouring)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of the water cycle (p. 7)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to think about where rain comes from and to trace the journey of a single drop of water from the ocean to a cloud to the ground. Students share ideas briefly, then open Textbook p. 7 to look at the water cycle diagram together. The teacher names each stage — evaporation, condensation, precipitation — without requiring students to memorise them yet.

Each group follows the activity instructions on Textbook p. 7: using a marker to draw the sun, clouds, trees, and arrows on the bag, then filling it one-third with coloured water and sealing it tightly. Groups fix the bags against a sunny window or take them to a sunny spot. Students watch the inside of the bag for a few minutes and begin filling the 'I Observe' column of their table, noting any moisture or droplets forming on the bag's inner surface.

While bags continue in the sun, the class discusses what they see happening and fills in the 'I Wonder' column — questions that the bag raises for them. The teacher guides the connection: the water warming inside mimics what the sun does to oceans and rivers; droplets on the upper inside of the bag mimic clouds; water dripping back down mimics rain.

Students write a brief explanation in their own words of what happens inside the bag and why it matches the diagram they saw. The teacher mentions the Fishing Cat of India's wetlands as an animal whose life depends entirely on this cycle continuing — linking the science to a living creature and inviting curiosity about freshwater animals.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple model to investigate a natural cycle and explain how the model represents the real process.
periods.section_context: Transparent sealed bag, coloured water, sun, evaporation inside bag, condensation on inner bag surface, water dripping back, water cycle diagram, Fishing Cat and freshwater wetlands.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Where in your model is the ocean? Where is the cloud? Where does the rain fall?' This keeps inquiry alive while the bag is in the sun. If students ask about snow and hail, invite them to think about what might happen if the 'cloud' were very cold.

periods.activity_title: Water Finds Its Way Down — Exploring Percolation
periods.textbook_anchor: Groundwater — Pouring water slowly into a transparent glass half-filled with soil and observing what happens (p. 9)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'When it rains heavily, where does all that water go?' Students share ideas. The teacher then asks them to think about what is under the ground — soil, rock, sand — and whether water can move through them. Students make a quick prediction in their notebooks: will water pass through soil easily, slowly, or not at all?

Students open Textbook p. 9 and carry out the activity: half-filling the glass with soil and slowly pouring water in using a spoon. They observe what happens — whether the water sits on top, moves through, or disappears — and record their observations. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Where is the water going? What would happen if you poured more?'

The class discusses findings and the teacher explains percolation — water moving downward through soil and rock layers until it collects as groundwater. Students look at Textbook p. 9 and tick the image that shows which surface type helps groundwater recharge (open lawn versus concrete or paved area). The teacher invites students to think about their school or neighbourhood: how much of the ground is open soil versus cement?

The teacher describes how paved city surfaces stop rain from reaching underground and raises the idea of soak pits and trees as helpers of recharge. Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one describing what they observed, one naming one thing in their locality that helps or hinders rainwater from going underground. The teacher asks students to notice, before their next walk, how much ground around them is open versus covered.

periods.implied_lo: Students can investigate how water moves through a permeable material and relate their findings to how groundwater is formed and replenished.
periods.section_context: Transparent glass, soil, water percolation, groundwater layers, wells, borewells, handpumps, concrete versus open surfaces, soak pits, trees aiding recharge, textbook images of surface types.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Draw out conversation about local wells or handpumps — ask whether anyone has seen a well drying up and what the family did. This brings the civic and traditional knowledge dimension to the science naturally, without labelling it.

periods.activity_title: Seeds as Rivers — Modelling Surface Water Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Surface Water — Pouring mustard seeds from the highest point of a crumpled-newspaper slope and observing how they move (p. 10)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of Indian rivers and their directions of flow (p. 13)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to think about a river they know — where it starts, where it goes, and whether it travels in a straight line. Students share briefly. The teacher then tells students they will model how rivers follow the shape of the land, using newspaper and seeds.

Students open Textbook p. 10 and follow the activity instructions: crumpling one newspaper sheet to create folds, laying the second sheet gently over it to form gentle slopes, then slowly pouring mustard seeds from the highest point. They observe and answer the three questions on the page — whether the seeds move in a straight line, whether they spread out, and where they collect.

Groups share their observations. The teacher connects the seed movement to river flow: rivers, like the seeds, follow the natural slopes of the land. Students then open to Textbook p. 13 and examine the map of India showing major rivers. Using the discussion prompt on p. 11, they talk about why some rivers flow toward the Bay of Bengal and others toward the Arabian Sea, relating it to the slopes they modelled with the seeds.

Students begin filling in the table on Textbook p. 13 — naming rivers and indicating which sea they flow toward. The teacher introduces the Luni River of Rajasthan as a river that ends in the Rann of Kutch and reaches no sea, inviting students to think about why. The teacher also briefly mentions Hiware Bazar — a village in Maharashtra where the whole community managed watershed and rainwater together — as an example of people working with the shape of their land.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model to explain how the shape of the land determines the direction and path of water flow, and apply this reasoning to map-based evidence.
periods.section_context: Crumpled newspaper, mustard seeds, river flow direction, slopes, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, map of Indian rivers, Luni River ending in Rann of Kutch, Hiware Bazar watershed management.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Could you change where your seeds collect by changing the shape of the crumpled paper?' This keeps the inquiry open and lets students test one more variation if time allows. When reading the map, encourage students to trace rivers with a finger before writing in the table.

periods.textbook_anchor: Surface Water — Observing rivers on the India map and filling in the table of river flow directions toward the Bay of Bengal or Arabian Sea (p. 13)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of major Indian rivers and direction of flow (p. 13)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 13 on the board (or asks students to open their own copies) and does a shared reading of the map key and direction arrows. The class identifies together which rivers are shown and the two bodies of water the rivers flow toward. Students recall from the mustard-seed activity that the land's shape decides a river's path.

Students work individually to complete the map-reading table on Textbook p. 13, recording the name of each river and ticking whether it flows toward the Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea. The teacher circulates, asking students to point to the river on the map before ticking the column, reinforcing that the answer comes from reading the map, not from memory.

The class reviews the completed table together. The teacher highlights the Luni River, which flows into the Rann of Kutch and reaches neither sea, and asks students to think about why this might be (arid land, no large slope to the coast). Students note this in their notebooks as a special case.

Students write one observation about the map in their own words — something they noticed about the pattern of river flow across India. The teacher asks: 'If you lived near a river that flowed into the Arabian Sea, what direction would that river generally be moving through your region?' This connects map reading to personal spatial reasoning.

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a simple country map to identify natural features and determine the direction of flow of major rivers using map symbols and directional cues.
periods.section_context: India map of major rivers, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, river flow direction table, Luni River and Rann of Kutch, directional reading of map features.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to use compass directions (north, east, west, south) when describing river flow if they are comfortable — this extends map-reading skill without being required. Prompt students who finish early to count how many rivers flow in each direction and decide which group is larger.

periods.activity_title: Water World — Adaptations and Food Chains in Freshwater
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in Water — Wax-crayon waterproofing activity: observing a water drop on plain paper versus wax-coated paper (p. 18)
materials: String or wool (for food chain game)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook information cards for freshwater organisms (pp. 14–19)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens a discussion: 'How is life in a pond different from life on land?' Students share ideas — gills instead of lungs, fins instead of legs. Students open Textbook p. 14 and complete the comparison table (animals on land versus animals in water) in pairs, drawing on what they already know and the information in the textbook.

Students carry out the wax-crayon activity on Textbook p. 18: placing a water drop on plain paper, observing it soak in; then colouring a section with a wax crayon and placing a water drop on the wax surface and observing how it beads and does not soak in. Students write their observation in their notebooks. The teacher connects this to aquatic plants such as the lotus and water lily — the waxy coating on their leaves does the same job, keeping them from becoming waterlogged.

The class plays the river food chain game from Textbook p. 19. The teacher distributes slips of paper and each student chooses a freshwater organism (small fish, big fish, frog, bird, crocodile, otter, etc.). Students think about what they eat and who eats them, and the teacher uses string to connect students who depend on each other. The class then discusses: what would happen if one organism disappeared from the chain?

Students write one sentence naming one freshwater organism, one adaptation it has, and one other organism it depends on for food. The teacher closes by asking: 'If we pollute a freshwater pond, which part of the food chain is harmed first, and does it stop there?' Students share a quick response before the unit ends.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe evidence of physical adaptations in aquatic organisms and explain how living things in a freshwater habitat depend on each other for survival.
periods.section_context: Land versus water animal comparison table, wax crayon on paper versus plain paper, water drop beading on wax, lotus and water lily waxy leaves, dragonfly, water scorpion, pond heron, freshwater turtle, water snake, reeds, water hyacinth, freshwater food chain game with string.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: During the food chain game, ask: 'If crocodiles disappeared, what changes for the fish?' This models ecological thinking beyond simple predator-prey pairs. Encourage students who name local freshwater organisms from their region — local names for fish, birds, or water plants are equally valid and enrich the activity.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Water — Reasoning, Designing, and Making
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Designing a water-conserving house or school (p. 20)
materials: Origami paper or square cut from notebook page

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 20 and work through the matching task and the first three written questions independently — matching ocean water, snow, steam, and rainwater to their properties; writing why most Earth water cannot be used; and explaining why large numbers of living beings cluster near water bodies. The teacher circulates and prompts where needed.

Students tackle the reasoning questions: what would happen if it did not rain in their region for two years, and what happens to rainwater in a forest compared to a city. The teacher invites two or three students to share their answers on the two-year drought question, making space for local knowledge — students from drought-prone areas or those who know traditional harvesting practices often have vivid, grounded answers.

Students use plain paper to sketch a water-conserving house or school (Textbook p. 20, question 6). They label at least three features that save water — such as a rooftop collection tank, a soak pit, a greywater garden, or open unpaved ground. The teacher moves around, asking each student to explain one design choice in their own words before they label it.

Students follow the origami fish steps on Textbook p. 20, folding their paper fish. When the fish is complete, the teacher invites students to name one freshwater creature their fish might be or one water body it might live in, linking the craft to the aquatic life they explored. The unit closes with the teacher asking: 'What is one thing you will do differently with water because of what you have thought about today?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply reasoning about water scarcity, the water cycle, and groundwater to design a practical solution for water conservation and justify their choices.
periods.section_context: Matching ocean water, snow, steam, rainwater to properties; reasons for unusable Earth water; living beings near water bodies; two-year drought consequences; rainwater in forest versus city; water-conserving house or school design; origami fish.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the design task, accept a simple labelled sketch — the quality of the reasoning behind each label matters more than artistic finish. Ask: 'Why did you choose to include that feature? What problem does it solve?' to push students from listing to justifying.

assessment_items.question_text: A student fills a large glass with water to show all the water on Earth. She uses a teaspoon to show how much of that water is freshwater. Which statement best explains why freshwater is so scarce?

options.label: A
options.text: Most of Earth's water is stored underground and cannot be reached at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water that cannot be used for drinking or farming.

options.label: C
options.text: Most of Earth's water evaporates into the sky and never comes back down.

options.label: D
options.text: Most of Earth's freshwater has already been used up by people and animals.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. Distractors target three specific misreadings of the scarcity idea.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between saltwater and freshwater sources and explain why freshwater is a limited and essential resource.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the idea of groundwater being hard to reach with an absolute inaccessibility claim — a partial truth overstated into an error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the water cycle (evaporation and return) with permanent loss — misunderstanding that evaporated water does return as rain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a consumption-based depletion story, misreading the chapter's message that scarcity is structural (saltwater dominance), not the result of overuse alone.

assessment_items.question_text: A student filled a dry steel glass with ice cubes. After a short time, she noticed tiny water droplets on the outside of the glass. She had not poured any water on the outside. Where did those droplets come from? Use what you observed about water's forms to explain.
expected_elements: States that the air around the glass contains water vapour (water in gaseous form).
Explains that the cold surface of the glass cooled the nearby air or water vapour.
Names the process: the water vapour turned into liquid water (condensation) on the glass surface.
Connects this to the idea that water can change between states — vapour, liquid, solid.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any response that correctly identifies air moisture (water vapour) as the source and cooling as the cause, even if the word 'condensation' is not used. A response that says 'water came through the glass' does not earn credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how the same material changes between states under different conditions and describe those changes in their own words.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Source identified as water vapour in the surrounding air.
Cooling of air or vapour by the cold glass named as the trigger.
Change of state from vapour to liquid described (condensation, in any words).
Explicit link to water existing in multiple forms.

assessment_items.question_text: A class made a sealed transparent bag model of the water cycle. They put coloured water inside, drew the sun and clouds on the bag, and placed it near a sunny window. After a while, droplets appeared on the upper inside of the bag and some water dripped back down. Explain what happened inside the bag and name the part of the real water cycle each step represents.
expected_elements: The water in the bag warmed up and turned to vapour — this represents evaporation.
The vapour cooled when it rose and touched the upper, cooler part of the bag, forming droplets — this represents condensation and cloud formation.
The droplets fell back down inside the bag — this represents precipitation (rain).
States that the process repeats continuously, matching the cyclic nature of the real water cycle.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept region-appropriate vocabulary for evaporation and condensation if a student describes the process accurately without the technical terms. Credit the cyclic point only if the student states or clearly implies that the water goes round again.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple model to investigate a natural cycle and explain how the model represents the real process.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Water warming and turning to vapour inside the bag — labelled as evaporation.
Vapour forming droplets on the upper bag surface — labelled as condensation or cloud formation.
Droplets falling back — labelled as rain or precipitation.
Recognition that the cycle repeats.

assessment_items.question_text: A student poured water slowly into a glass half-filled with soil and watched it disappear into the soil. Which surface in a neighbourhood would allow rainwater to do the same thing and help refill groundwater?

options.label: A
options.text: A wide concrete road with drains on the side.

options.label: B
options.text: A paved courtyard made of flat stone tiles.

options.label: C
options.text: An open grassy lawn with loose soil underneath.

options.label: D
options.text: A rooftop terrace covered with waterproof coating.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. All three distractors represent impermeable surfaces discussed in the Groundwater section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can investigate how water moves through a permeable material and relate their findings to how groundwater is formed and replenished.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.A: Recognises roads as human-made but does not connect the impermeable surface to blocked infiltration — a partial understanding that stops at identification.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses smooth natural stone (still impermeable) with open soil — suggests the student equates 'not concrete' with 'water can pass through'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects a rooftop because it collects rainwater, confusing surface collection with underground percolation — a different water-conservation idea applied to the wrong question.

assessment_items.question_text: In class, students crumpled a sheet of newspaper and poured mustard seeds from the highest point. The seeds spread out and collected in low areas rather than moving in a straight line. How does this model explain why some Indian rivers flow toward the Bay of Bengal while others flow toward the Arabian Sea?
expected_elements: The seeds (like rivers) follow the slope of the land downward rather than moving in a straight line.
The direction the seeds travel is decided by where the high points and low points of the crumpled paper are.
In the same way, rivers flow in the direction the land slopes — toward the Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea depending on which side of India they start.
The model shows that landform shape (not human choice) determines river direction.
assessment_items.annotation: Credit any response that clearly links the slope of the newspaper to the direction of seed movement, and then transfers this logic to the India map. Naming specific rivers is not required but is a positive indicator.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model to explain how the shape of the land determines the direction and path of water flow, and apply this reasoning to map-based evidence.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Seeds follow the slope downward, not a straight line — connected to river behaviour.
High and low points of the paper determine seed direction — connected to India's landform heights.
River direction toward Bay of Bengal or Arabian Sea explained by which side of India's slope the river begins on.
Conclusion that landform shape, not chance, governs river flow direction.

assessment_items.question_text: A student read the map of Indian rivers on Textbook p. 13. She noted that the Luni River of Rajasthan does not flow into either the Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea. Which statement best explains what makes the Luni River different from most other Indian rivers shown on the map?

options.label: A
options.text: The Luni River flows underground instead of on the surface, so it cannot reach the sea.

options.label: B
options.text: The Luni River ends in the Rann of Kutch and does not have a continuous slope that carries it to a sea.

options.label: C
options.text: The Luni River is a saltwater river, so it is not shown flowing into a freshwater body.

options.label: D
options.text: The Luni River flows northward, which is opposite to all other Indian rivers on the map.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. All distractors reflect specific confusions a student might bring after the map-reading activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a simple country map to identify natural features and determine the direction of flow of major rivers using map symbols and directional cues.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the Luni's unusual end destination with a groundwater river, mixing the Groundwater section's ideas with map reading.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Imports the saltwater versus freshwater distinction from the chapter's opening section and misapplies it to explain a directional map observation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misreads the map direction — the Luni does not flow northward; this shows the student has not traced the river carefully on the map.

assessment_items.question_text: A lotus plant lives with its roots underwater and its leaves floating on the surface. A student coated a piece of paper with wax crayon and found that a water drop rolled off rather than soaking in. How does this observation help explain how a lotus leaf survives in a water body? In your answer, describe what the wax does, what it does for the lotus leaf, and why this matters for the plant's survival.
look_for: Clearly states that the wax (or waxy coating) prevents water from soaking into the surface — it repels water.
Connects the wax-paper observation directly to the lotus leaf's waxy surface and explains that the leaf stays dry on top even though it floats on water.
Explains at least one survival benefit: the dry surface allows the leaf to carry out its functions (absorbing sunlight, gas exchange) without being waterlogged.
Shows an understanding that this is an adaptation — the lotus has this feature because it lives in water, not by accident.
Optional, bonus indicator: mentions another aquatic plant (water lily, water hyacinth) as having a similar feature, showing the student generalises the observation.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response draws a clear line from the classroom wax-paper observation to the lotus leaf, names at least one functional benefit, and uses the word 'adaptation' or describes the concept without the word. A weak response lists features of the lotus without connecting them to the wax activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe evidence of physical adaptations in aquatic organisms and explain how living things in a freshwater habitat depend on each other for survival.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

look_for: Wax repels water — water beads and rolls off rather than soaking in.
Lotus leaf has a natural waxy coating that works the same way.
The leaf stays functional (dry on top) despite living on the water surface.
Framing this as an adaptation to a watery habitat, not just a coincidence.
Bonus: generalisation to other aquatic plants with similar coatings.

assessment_items.task: Design a house or school that uses water wisely. On plain paper, draw and label your design. Include at least three features that save or reuse water, and for each feature write one sentence explaining what problem it solves.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: Where does rainwater go when it falls on the roof or the ground? What happens to water after you wash hands or vegetables? Where could plants get water without using a tap? Draw your building, add labels for each water-saving feature, and write one sentence of explanation next to each label.
format_of_output: Labelled sketch of a house or school
At least three named water-saving features
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally relevant water-saving features — rooftop rainwater collection, soak pits, kitchen-water gardens, open unpaved ground, low-flow taps, reuse of washing water for plants. Regional variation in what counts as practical is expected and all reasonable answers are correct. Award full credit for three clearly labelled features each with a coherent explanation, regardless of artistic quality.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply reasoning about water scarcity, the water cycle, and groundwater to design a practical solution for water conservation and justify their choices.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can synthesise ideas about water scarcity, the water cycle, groundwater recharge, and surface water to propose and justify practical conservation measures — moving from knowing facts to applying them in a design context.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts three real-world water moments (rain landing, washing water, plant watering) to help students who are unsure where to start. A student who ignores the scaffold and produces three strong labelled features with explanations still meets the criteria fully.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three features each with a clear causal explanation linking the feature to a specific water problem (e.g., 'A soak pit next to the building lets rainwater go underground and refill the well instead of running away on the road'). Weak: a drawing with labels but no explanatory sentences, or explanations that are too vague ('saves water') without saying how.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw may describe their design in words with a simple list of features and explanations. Students in drought-prone areas may propose traditional features (open wells, check dams) — these are equally valid and should be celebrated. Students from flood-prone areas may include flood-diversion or storage features.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled design sketch with written justifications
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The design-and-justify format mirrors the chapter's emphasis on moving from understanding to action, and lets students from different regions propose locally meaningful solutions.
